slot.brief: Show a dip circle / place with given horizontal and vertical components (or dip angle); use tan(dip) = Bv/Bh to find a missing component or the total field.

stem: At a place, the Earth's magnetic field has the horizontal component shown in the figure and a dip angle of $45^\circ$. What is the magnitude of its vertical component?

verdicts.working: The dip angle satisfies \(\tan 45^\circ = B_V/B_H\). Thus \(B_V = 4\times10^{-5}\,\text{T}\).

working:
$\tan\delta=\dfrac{B_V}{B_H}$.
$B_V=B_H\tan45^\circ=4\times10^{-5}\ \text{T}$. Independent check: The dip angle satisfies \(\tan 45^\circ = B_V/B_H\). Thus \(B_V = 4\times10^{-5}\,\text{T}\).
solution:
The dip angle relates the vertical and horizontal components by $\tan\delta=\dfrac{B_V}{B_H}$.
$$B_V=B_H\tan45^\circ=4\times10^{-5}\ \text{T}$$

draft.stem: At a place, the Earth's magnetic field has the horizontal component shown in the figure and a dip angle of $45^\circ$. What is the magnitude of its vertical component?

figure.description: Draw a simple dip-angle vector diagram. From a common origin, draw a horizontal arrow pointing right labelled $B_H=4\times10^{-5}\ \text{T}$. Draw a vertical arrow pointing downward labelled $B_V$. Draw a diagonal arrow from the origin pointing down and right to represent the Earth's total field. Mark the angle between the diagonal arrow and the horizontal rightward arrow as $45^\circ$. Label the diagram with the usual horizontal and vertical component directions; do not give a value for $B_V$.

draft.distractor_notes: A: halves the horizontal component; C: calculates the total field; D: doubles the horizontal component.
